Ingest Schedule I recipient aliases as observed names and addresses

Source: R/md-ingest-schedi.R
md_ingest_schedi.Rd

Form 990 Schedule I Part II is where a non-PF filer lists every grant it made to a US organisation, with the recipient's name, address and EIN. That last field is what makes it unlike every other source here: it is a large set of (name variant, address variant) to EIN observations, written by third parties, in the register a grantmaker actually uses.

Usage

md_ingest_schedi(
  version = "v2_2",
  years = NULL,
  con = NULL,
  min_corroborators = 1L,
  guard = TRUE
)

Arguments

version

Pinned schedi version, e.g. "v2_2".

years

Years to load. Defaults to every file present.

con

A connection from md_db().

min_corroborators

Drop groups written by fewer than this many distinct filers. 1 keeps everything; filtering belongs in the spec, so the default loads all of it.

guard

Run md_guard_observed() on the loaded rows. Flags are only as good as the first-party names already loaded, so re-run it once the BMF and return headers are in.

Value

Row counts, invisibly.

Details

The BMF gives one legal name per EIN. This gives many observed names, and it is the source pfmatch/dev/AUDIT-FINDINGS.md named as the missing piece for brand-versus-legal-name matching.

Corroboration is the trust signal

Rows are collapsed to one per (ein, name_key, city, state, zip5) and carry n_corroborators, the count of distinct filers who wrote that string for that EIN. One filer's typo and a brand name fifty foundations independently use are both "observed names"; only the corroborator count separates them. It becomes a spec filter (§5) rather than a threshold baked into a script.

The pairing link

A grantmaker wrote a name and an address together, and that pairing is real information. Each observed address carries the name_id it was seen with, so the compiler emits roughly k + m rows per EIN rather than k x m (§8). Losing the link is what turns a useful source into a row explosion.

Grouping on a key, storing the raw string

Deduplication needs some normalisation or trivial punctuation differences become separate variants. Rows are grouped on the light key (md_light_key(): accents and & spelled out, uppercased, punctuation dropped, whitespace collapsed) - but the stored name_raw is the most frequently written raw form within the group, so the database still holds a string a filer actually typed rather than a normalised reconstruction. np_normalize() derived columns are built from that raw string later, exactly as for BMF rows.

Wrong names on the right line

A filer's own EIN written for its grantee, a denomination's central EIN written for a congregation, a fiscal sponsor's EIN written for its projects, 000000000 and SEE SCHEDULE O: all are on Schedule I, often by many filers. Rows are kept and flagged by md_guard_observed(); see dev/OBSERVED-NAME-GUARDS.md for how many and how corroborated they are.
